name: CoolSculpting Elite

lead: CoolSculpting Elite is Allergan's newer fat-freezing system. It chills stubborn pockets of fat through the skin so areas such as the chin, abdomen, flanks and thighs look slimmer without surgery.

Controlled cooling of subcutaneous fat (cryolipolysis) causes fat cells to die off over several weeks, and the body clears them. Reviews report modest reductions in fat thickness and high satisfaction, though data quality is described as low.

paras: Applicators are placed on the skin over the target area in a clinic session, with no incision or downtime. Results build over a few weeks, and people use it to sharpen contour on specific spots rather than for overall weight loss.

Redness, numbness, swelling and bruising are common and usually resolve in weeks. A rare complication, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, enlarges the treated fat and may need surgery; it has been reported in about 0.12 to 1 percent of cases.

chain: Fat cells die off over weeks
angle.text: People use fat freezing to shrink stubborn pockets such as the belly or flanks and sharpen body contour without surgery. Cooling kills fat cells over a few weeks, leaving a smaller local pocket. Studies document modest local fat reduction.

lead: CoolSculpting Elite is a version of the CoolSculpting cryolipolysis system, a non-invasive procedure that reduces localized subcutaneous fat by controlled cooling through the skin. It is made by Allergan Aesthetics, which acquired the CoolSculpting brand from Zeltiq in 2017 [1][2].

People use it to slim stubborn pockets of fat that persist despite diet and exercise, such as under the chin, along the jawline, the flanks, abdomen, thighs and upper arms. The FDA has cleared cryolipolysis for several of these areas, including the submental area and jawline, which makes it relevant to facial contour and neck definition as well as body shape [1][3].

Reviews describe cryolipolysis as producing measurable but modest fat-layer reductions with high patient satisfaction. A rare complication, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which treated fat enlarges, has been reported [1][4][5].
infobox: Submental, jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen, thighs, under buttocks [1]

paras: Cryolipolysis, often called fat freezing, uses cold applied through the skin to reduce fat in a targeted area. Zeltiq Aesthetics developed the technology and introduced it in the US in 2010 as CoolSculpting; Allergan Aesthetics acquired it in 2017 [1]. CoolSculpting Elite is a later system from Allergan Aesthetics [2]. Treatments are delivered by clinicians in sessions using applicators placed over the area.

The idea behind cryolipolysis grew out of observations that cold can selectively injure fat. In 1902 Hochsinger described firm nodules under children's chins after acute cold injury, and in 1970 Epstein and Oren reported "popsicle panniculitis" in an infant who developed a hard red nodule and fat loss in the cheek after sucking on a popsicle.[6] Manstein and colleagues drew on these observations to develop cryolipolysis; their 2008 pig study showed fat reduction without skin injury or significant changes in serum lipids or liver function, and a 2009 pig study by Zelickson and colleagues confirmed the result.[6]

The technology reached the US market through Zeltiq as CoolSculpting in 2010, and Allergan Aesthetics acquired the brand in 2017.[1] According to a 2015 Aesthetic Surgery Journal paper, FDA clearances came for the flanks in 2010, the abdomen in 2012 and the thighs in 2014; use on the back, arms, inner thighs and chest was off-label at that time.[6] The FDA now lists additional areas, including the submental area and jawline.[1]

Reviews describe cryolipolysis as exposing fat to cold that triggers apoptosis of fat cells while sparing the surrounding tissue; macrophages then clear the damaged cells, thinning the fat layer [7]. Researchers have examined tissue effects in controlled studies, including immunohistochemical analysis of treated fat in adult women and a pilot study on conversion of white adipose tissue [8][9]. The same 2023 review says further work is needed to understand the mechanism and efficacy by treatment area [7].

Early systems used vacuum applicators that draw tissue between cooling plates, with a session of about an hour; a conformable-surface applicator that works without vacuum was developed so that fibrous, non-pinchable fat on the lateral thigh could be treated, with a longer session of about two hours.[6] In that 2015 thigh study, ultrasound showed a mean fat-layer reduction of 2.6 mm versus the untreated control thigh at the final follow-up, and 86 percent of patients said results met or exceeded expectations.[6] Follow-up in the study was at about two and four months.[6]

A 2015 systematic review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery covered 19 studies and reported average caliper reductions of 14.67 to 28.5 percent and ultrasound-measured reductions of 10.3 to 25.5 percent, with no significant effect on lipid levels or liver function tests; side effects were mild and short term [4]. Wikipedia summarises this review and a 2023 review of 18 studies, which found ultrasound-measured fat reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm and described the effects as safe but modest with low data quality [1].

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in Obesity Reviews included 30 studies and 3,158 participants. At 12 weeks after treatment, pooled analyses showed lower body mass index (mean difference -1.80), waist-to-hip ratio, abdominal circumference (-3.56 cm) and suprailiac fat thickness (-5.22 mm) compared with baseline; satisfaction was 80.4 percent, and adverse events were reported in 49.5 percent of treatments, which the abstract does not characterise further in the available text [5].

A split-body trial examined abdominal fat changes over 12 weeks after a single unilateral session [10]. A randomised split-body trial reported that active heating after cryolipolysis reduced both efficacy and side effects [11]. A multicentre trial examined fat reduction on the lateral chest wall after mastectomy [12]. Neck-focused reviews place cryolipolysis among non-surgical options for submental fullness [13].

Redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain are common and usually resolve within weeks [1]. Paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which treated fat enlarges, is reported in about 0.12 to 1.0 percent of cases depending on the study, and treatment may be surgical, such as liposuction or abdominoplasty [1]. A 2015 review noted a single case of it among the studies reviewed [4]. A case report has described morphea, a skin-hardening condition, after cryolipolysis [14], and a Hacker News thread discussed a paper on paradoxical adipose hyperplasia [15]. A retrospective chart review of 3,262 patients and 18,203 cycles of CoolSculpting and CoolSculpting Elite examined real-world use and adverse events [16].

Eligibility criteria in the thigh study excluded people with known cryoglobulinemia, cold urticaria or paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, and people who had surgery or other non-surgical fat reduction in the area in the prior six months; these were study criteria rather than a complete list of contraindications.[6]

Cryolipolysis is promoted by clinics as an alternative to liposuction for local fat, and the reviews position it as nonsurgical body contouring [7][17]. Face and neck appearance programmes combine it with other treatments: a registered study evaluated satisfaction after combined onabotulinumtoxinA, Juvederm filler, Kybella, CoolSculpting Elite and skincare products [3].

A retrospective single-clinic study examined patient satisfaction, recommendation rate and comfort with a cleared cryolipolysis system [2]. Registered trials include phase 4 studies of CoolSculpting Elite for non-invasive fat reduction (NCT04897867, 110 participants, started 2021) and for the submental, inner thigh and back/bra areas (NCT07122583, 102 participants, started 2025), a 15-person study combining CoolSculpting with CoolTone for the banana roll area, and a 130-person facial-contouring study combining several aesthetic treatments (NCT06783621) [18][19][20][3]. Systematic reviews and randomised trials of earlier cryolipolysis systems are summarised above [4][5][11].

timeline.event: CoolSculpting introduced in the US by Zeltiq [1].
Systematic review of 19 cryolipolysis studies published [4].
Phase 4 study of CoolSculpting Elite begins (NCT04897867) [18].
Meta-analysis of 30 studies (3,158 participants) and a real-world review of 18,203 cycles are published [5][16].
